title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening (scottaaronson.blog)
comments: AI is good at analytic a priori things like axiomatic math and that's good, but it doesn't follow that it will write the Encyclopedia Galactica or "solve" other fields, much less that it will play the sci-fi role and kills us all. It might; it might not. It just doesn't follow from a bunch of math proofs.I think mathies are really wedded to the notion that they are the queen of the sciences, and I even agree with that, but the entire corpus of "science" before and up to the start of the scientific revolution was based on notion that it would be like Euclid. Major philosophers of the three major Abrahamic faiths wrote works along those lines. And so people like Galileo were considered cranks because they violated the axioms of that kind of system. People didn't even believe in non-Euclidean geometry at all until ~200 ya.But it's not true. There's more to reality than that kind of system. I'm not saying it cannot do it one day, but Aarsonson is more or less thinking we're in the singularity because his field has been solved and really showed his hand in a reply to a troll comment. Yes, it's glib to ask "what's all this for" and, again, I love math, I find math beautiful, and I have studied a lot of it.But even a major break in some of our crypto systems isn't the singularity. It's sort of like Y2K all over again.The world ending because my job has been replaced is even a meme, it's just happening to people with credentials and a large vocabulary now.reply

My anecdata on this from what I’ve seen at work is that the results really depend on the human driving the agent (at least that’s the case now, ask me again next week and it may have changed). A skilled developer can get better code out of Claude than an unskilled developer because they’re able to break down the problem in ways that enable the agent to approach the solution more efficiently and effectively. In many ways it’s about asking the right questions. Adequate work can be accomplished by starting with “implement FUBAR-420” and, to be honest, for most of us, adequate is fine. On the other hand, for creating something from scratch, it takes a lot of understanding of the problem and solution spaces. title: 1Password Security Incident (1password.com)
comments: This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.reply

> You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.You kinda have to wonder if this is necessary or true. I can’t say I’ve seen the rate of significant product improvements from SaaS providers increase this year (for 1Password in particular, I can’t think of one thing that had changed this year in the product).However there has undoubtedly been an uptick in major outages and security incidents that have accompanied the increased rate of change.reply

minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure.
A .pgdb directory is the database:
its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it,
and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it.
A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.

minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with
h9, used as a Zig library.
h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor,
with h9's Plan 9 kernel answering their system calls.
There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.

The demo downloads about 35 MB.
It needs JavaScript Promise Integration,
which Chrome and Edge have from version 137;
other browsers are getting it.
It can also be opened on its own page.

title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (In 3 Minutes) (friedgil.com)
comments: The article says “This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication.”This is implying that if P=NP then there must be a polynomial time algorithm for finding the permanent. But that isn’t known to be true. It would be consistent with all known results if P=NP but computing the permanent is still not possible in polynomial time.Finding the permanent of a 0/1 matrix in polynomial time is stronger than P=NP; it would let you count the number of solutions to NP problems in polynomial time.reply

Horizontal overflow is so annoying on mobile and 10x worse when it persists in reader view. There's no reason why your equations shouldn't either have overflow-x: auto; which will give them their own horizontal scrollbar instead of abusing the whole page, or just let them wrap, possibly with an indent in the next line/s.reply
Can someone say how proving P=NP will automatically allow us to crack RSA? Like if we have a public key, just by using the proof of P=NP, can we easily get the private key from it?reply

Depending on the proof of P=NP and what you mean by "easily". In TCS, anything polynomial is considered "easily" so it could easily be the case that some ridiculous polynomial is implied with some ridiculous constants.Suppose the proof of P=NP were not constructive, then Levin's universal search algorithm automatically gives us an algorithm that finds the factors in polynomial time. This would satisfy some definition of "easily" from above. However, if you take a look at Levin's universal search, it quickly becomes apparent the constants involved are truly galactic and not worth even thinking about in a practical sense.If the proof of P=NP were constructive but gave some incredibly high degree polynomial or something with incredibly high constants, then we might be more wary. We would be able to get get factors in polynomial time but it would still be "hard" in a practical sense to get the private key but it becomes exceedingly difficult to guarantee that there isn't some practically efficient algorithm. Proving fine grained lower bounds like this has been difficult to say the least.If the proof of P=NP were constructive and efficient, then we would easily be able to get the private key.reply

I’m not qualified to answer this.(Well my qualification is this –  I took a semester of Theory of Computation class about a decade ago and barely managed to pass without screwing up my scholarship in the foreign country I was studying in. Today I write PHP during my day job..)One way to try to get the private key is to try all possibilities. For an RSA key with 4096 bits, there are 2^4096 possible keys, which I’m told is greater than the number of atoms in the universe.So you see, this is a O(2^n) operation. ie., the algorithm is “exponential”.You’ll never finish checking all those combinations before the universe ends, or at least not before the Sun explodes and the Earth ceases to exist as we know it.Unless you’re really really lucky and a key you try during your lifetime happens to be the actual private key. But the likelihood of that happening is practically zero because of the sheer number of possibilities.The point is, you have to exhaustively check all possible keys. Exponential.P=NP means there exists a polynomial time (O(n^k)) algorithm to find the private key. ie., it can be found relatively quickly.This is all I know. I skipped a lot of details. Experts can chime in.reply

I like your explanation, but you merely said that a high number of possibilities means it takes a long high time to break it. This is true independently of whether such high number is obtained as an exponential (2^n) or a polynomial (k*n, with k very big).I think it's more about growth: if we ever build a supercomputer that can break RSA in a reasonal time, we will bump that 4096 a bit to still be safe. In the case of exponential algorithm like 2^n, if you increase n by 1, you double the breaking time. In the other case you have to double n to get the same effect.So, it's not about how hard it is to break it, it's about how fast can we make it harder.reply

It wouldn’t.  If P=NP then many problems we think are hard (ie currently require exponential time) would in fact be solvable in polynomial time.  But such a polynomial time algorithm might be “galactic” in the sense that the constants are so astronomically large that in practice the algorithm would not be faster than current methods.Note that this is not widely believed to be likely, because usually if a problem is in P, then usually further work can improve constants considerably, but it is a possibility that there is a certain class of problems in P that are “galacticly” polynomial.reply
Proving P=NP is theoretical, for starters. It would be an important finding, but it wouldn't immediately break RSA encryption.reply
Unless someone presents a constructive proof, an actual algorithm.reply

> if we have a public key, just by using the proof of P=NP, can we easily get the private key from it?There's a couple more steps, but since we have AI, I wouldn't say it would be easy per se, but it goes from being actually impossible to "okay, maybe with a lot of effort". Right now, it's impossible for anybody to snoop or alter the TLS connection to my bank that's encrypted with a 4k RSA key. To go from impossible to "maybe the CIA/NSA if they really cared" would be world changing. Nevermind that me talking to my bank is not that interesting to them, the mere possibility upends a lot of assumptions about the world that computer people have.It wouldn't be automatic, but a CIA agent with access to Claude and enough tokens could then do it.reply

From the outside it feels like something substantial changed in how they approach everything, but the weird part is how it’s coming at the worst possible time for them to be appearing like the lesser deal. Did they finally get the internal marching orders to turn the profitability knob up and ignore everything else?reply
